studies.Reference: Higher intakes of vegetables and vegetable-related nutrients are associated with lower endometrial cancer risks.
studies.Authors: Yeh M, Moysich KB, Jayaprakash V, Rodabaugh KJ, Graham S, Brasure JR, McCann SE
studies.exposure_measurement_supporting_text: Self-reported dietary and other epidemiologic data were collected by questionnaire.

extraction_supporting_text.sample_size: 541 women with histologically confirmed EC and 541 women with an intact uterus and noncancer diagnoses
extraction_supporting_text.effect_direction: significant inverse associations for women in the highest vs. lowest quartiles of intake of ... vitamin E
extraction_supporting_text.exposure_definition: intakes of selected food groups and nutrients ... vitamin E

studies.Reference: [Diet, smoking and reproductive history as risk factor for cervical cancer].
studies.Authors: Atalah E, Urteaga C, Rebolledo A, Villegas RA, Medina E, Csendes A
studies.exposure_measurement_supporting_text: Food and nutrient intakes were assessed by a food frequency questionnaire considering 58 antioxidant rich food items.

extraction_supporting_text.sample_size: A matched case control study of 170 cases and 340 controls.
extraction_supporting_text.effect_size: Multivariate analysis model showed a protective effect for vegetable and vitamin E consumption (odds ratio of 0.6 with confidence intervals of 0.5 to 0.8 p < 0.001)
extraction_supporting_text.effect_direction: High intakes of vegetables, fruits, beta carotene, vitamin C, E and fiber were associated with a lower risk of cervical cancer

headline.funnel_interpretation: Insufficient studies to perform formal publication bias testing.
headline.results_interpretation: The pooled analysis of 2 studies yielded an overall effect size of 0.59 (95% CI: 0.46–0.75), suggesting that vitamin_e is associated with a lower risk of uterine cancer. These findings were supported by low between-study heterogeneity (I² = 23.01%), indicating consistent findings across the included studies.
